doc_name: Assassination of Juvénal Habyarimana and Cyprien Ntaryamira
text: On the evening of 6 April 1994, the aircraft carrying Rwandan president Juvénal Habyarimana and Burundian president Cyprien Ntaryamira, both Hutu, was shot down with surface-to-air missiles as it prepared to land in Kigali, Rwanda; both were killed. The assassination triggered the Rwandan genocide, one of the bloodiest events of the late 20th century. Responsibility for the attack is disputed, with most theories pointing to either the Tutsi rebel Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF) or government-aligned Hutu Power followers opposed to negotiations with the RPF. The Rwandan Civil War began in 1990 when the RPF, dominated by the Tutsi ethnic group, invaded northern Rwanda from Uganda. Most of the RPF fighters were refugees or sons of refugees who had fled ethnic purges by the Hutu government during the Rwandan revolution. The attempt to overthrow the government failed, though the RPF maintained control of a border region. As the war reached a stalemate, peace negotiations began in May 1992, resulting in the signing of the Arusha Accords in August 1993 to establish a power-sharing government. The war radicalized internal opposition, with the RPF's show of force strengthening support for the "Hutu Power" ideology, which portrayed the RPF as an alien force intent on reinstating the Tutsi monarchy and enslaving the Hutus. The Coalition for the Defense of the Republic (CDR) embraced these racist principles, known as the Hutu Ten Commandments, and led to the collapse of the first Habyarimana government in July 1993 when Prime Minister Dismas Nsengiyaremye criticized the president for delaying a peace agreement. Habyarimana dismissed Nsengiyaremye and appointed Agathe Uwilingiyimana, who was seen as less sympathetic to the RPF, in his place. The main opposition parties split into factions: one committed to Hutu Power and another, labeled "moderate," seeking a negotiated settlement. Uwilingiyimana was unable to form a coalition, making ratification of the Arusha Accords impossible. The CDR, which openly called for ethnic cleansing of the Tutsi, was entirely unrepresented in the Accords. The security situation worsened throughout 1993, with armed Hutu militias attacking Tutsis and high-ranking Hutu Power figures considering how to turn the security forces to genocide. In February 1994, Roméo Dallaire, head of the United Nations Assistance Mission for Rwanda (UNAMIR), warned his superiors that political discussions were running out of time due to the risk of catastrophic consequences. In early April 1994, the United Nations Security Council faced a dispute between the United States and non-permanent members over UNAMIR. Despite a classified February Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) analysis predicting half a million deaths if the Arusha process failed, the U.S. sought to reduce its international commitments following the Somalia debacle and lobbied to end the mission. A compromise extending UNAMIR's mandate for three more months was reached on the evening of 5 April. Habyarimana was traveling regionally: on 4 April he flew to Zaire to meet with President Mobutu Sese Seko, and on 6 April to Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, for a one-day summit convened by Tanzanian President Ali Hassan Mwinyi. For the return trip, Habyarimana offered to take Tanzania's Ambassador to Rwanda, Saleh Tambwe, with him, then extended the offer to President Ntaryamira, who accepted, preferring Habyarimana's faster Dassault Falcon 50 to his own transport. Several Burundian ministers joined the flight, and as a result, Tambwe was not brought on board. According to interim Prime Minister Jean Kambanda's testimony to the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR), Mobutu had warned Habyarimana not to go to Dar es Salaam on 6 April, claiming the warning came from a senior official at the Élysée Palace in Paris. Mobutu linked this warning to the suicide of François de Grossouvre, a senior official working for President François Mitterrand, who died by suicide on 7 April after learning about the downing of the Falcon. Shortly before 8:20 pm local time (18:20 UTC), the presidential jet circled Kigali International Airport once before final approach in clear skies. A weekly flight by a Belgian C-130 Hercules carrying UNAMIR troops returning from leave had been scheduled to land before the presidential jet but was waved off to give the president priority. A surface-to-air missile struck one of the wings of the Dassault Falcon, followed by a second missile hitting its tail. The plane erupted into flames mid-air and crashed into the garden of the presidential palace, exploding on impact. The plane carried three French crew members and nine passengers. The attack was witnessed by numerous people. One of two Belgian officers in Kanombe saw and heard the first missile climb into the sky, saw a red flash, and heard the aircraft engine stop, followed by another missile. He immediately called Major de Saint-Quentin, who advised him to protect his Belgian comrades. Another Belgian officer in an unused airport control tower saw the lights of an approaching aircraft, a light rising from the ground, and the aircraft lights going out, followed by a second light rising from the same place and the plane turning into a falling ball of fire. He immediately radioed his company commander, who confirmed with the operational control tower that the plane was the presidential aircraft. A Rwandan soldier in Camp Kanombe recalled that the president's engine sound was different from other planes; he saw a projectile, a ball of flame, and the plane go down. As the leader of the bloc, he told soldiers to get up and said, "Kinani has been shot down," though they initially denied it. He then put on his uniform and heard the bugle sound. A Rwandan officer cadet at the airport, listening to Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines, heard the announcer state the presidential jet was coming in to land, then the broadcast abruptly switched to classical music. All twelve aboard the Falcon were killed. The French aircraft crew were: The crash caused chaos on the ground. Presidential Guards, who had been waiting to escort the president home, threatened people with their weapons. Twenty Belgian peacekeepers stationed along the airport perimeter were surrounded and some disarmed. The airport was closed, and the circling Belgian Hercules was diverted to Nairobi. In Camp Kanombe, the bugle call immediately after the crash was interpreted as a sign that the RPF had attacked the camp. Soldiers rushed to their armories, and the para-commando brigade Commandos de recherche et d'action en profondeur assembled on the parade ground at around 9:00 pm, while other units gathered elsewhere. At least one witness reported gunfire in Kanombe about an hour after the crash, and munitions explosions were initially reported. The senior officer for the Kigali operational zone called the Ministry of Defence; Defence Minister Augustin Bizimana was out of the country, and the officer who took the call failed to reach Colonel Théoneste Bagosora, who was at a reception with UNAMIR's Bangladeshi officers. The news of the crash, initially reported as an explosion of UNAMIR's ammunition dump, was relayed to UNAMIR Force Commander Dallaire, who ordered Kigali sector commander Luc Marchal to send a patrol to the crash site. Numerous people called UNAMIR for information, including Prime Minister Agathe Uwilingiyimana and Lando Ndasingwa. Uwilingiyimana informed Dallaire she was trying to gather her cabinet but many ministers were afraid to leave their families. She reported that all hardline ministers had disappeared. Dallaire asked her to confirm it was the president's plane, and called UNAMIR political head Jacques-Roger Booh-Booh. Uwilingiyimana confirmed it was the president's jet and that he was presumed on board. She also requested UNAMIR assistance in regaining control of the political situation, as she was legally next in line of succession, though some moderate ministers had already fled. At 9:18 pm, Presidential Guards, described as "nervous and dangerous," established a roadblock near the Hotel Méridien. Several other roadblocks had been set up in advance for Habyarimana's arrival. A patrol of UNAMIR Belgian soldiers sent to investigate the crash site was stopped at a Presidential Guards roadblock at 9:35 pm, disarmed, and sent to the airport. The para-commando brigade was ordered to collect bodies from the crash site, and UN peacekeepers were prevented from accessing it. Akingeneye was quickly recovered, but most corpses were damaged beyond immediate recognition. Habyarimana was identified lying in a flowerbed at about 21:30 on 6 April, while Ntaryamira was recognized at about 03:00 on 7 April. One Rwandan advisor was identified after his wife told the search party about his clothing. The last to be identified were the French aircrew, discovered at dawn outside the palace gardens. The bodies were taken into the Presidential Palace living room. Plans were initially made to take them to the hospital, but renewed conflict made this difficult, so the two presidents' bodies were stored in a freezer at a nearby army barracks. Two French soldiers arrived at the crash site and asked to be given the flight data recorder once it was recovered. The whereabouts of the flight data recorder were later unknown. The French military contacted Dallaire and offered to investigate the crash, which he refused immediately. A Rwandan colonel who called the army command about 40 minutes after the crash was told there was no confirmation that the president was dead. About half an hour later, at roughly 9:30, the situation remained confused, though it appeared clear the presidential aircraft had exploded and had likely been hit by a missile. News arrived that Major-General Déogratias Nsabimana, the army chief of staff, had been on the plane. Officers realized they needed to appoint a new chief of staff and began a meeting to decide who should take the role. Col. Bagosora joined them soon afterward. At about 10:00 pm, Ephrem Rwabalinda, the government liaison officer to UNAMIR, called Dallaire to inform him that a crisis committee was about to meet. After informing his superiors in New York, Dallaire went to attend the meeting, where he found Bagosora in charge. Observers feared that President Ntaryamira's death would lead to widespread violence in Burundi, as had occurred when his predecessor, Melchior Ndadaye, was assassinated in October 1993. However, unlike in Rwanda, the situation in Burundi remained peaceful. The Burundian government declared the plane crash an accident, and President of the National Assembly Sylvestre Ntibantunganya made a television broadcast, flanked by the minister of defence and the army chief of staff, appealing for calm. Several hundred Tutsis marched through the capital to celebrate the deaths of the presidents. Diplomats reported that most Burundians believed the assassination targeted Habyarimana, not Ntaryamira. On 16 April, a requiem mass was held for Ntaryamira at the Regina Mundi Cathedral in Bujumbura, attended by thousands, and he and his two ministers were buried in a state funeral. Ntibantunganya succeeded Ntaryamira as President of Burundi and believed Ntaryamira's death was "by the facts of circumstance" and that he was not targeted. In response to the assassination, President Mwinyi declared three days of national mourning in Tanzania and sent messages of condolence to the Rwandan and Burundian governments and the families of the deceased presidents. He wrote in his memoirs that the Tanzanian government was "shocked" by the downing of the plane. A group of about 70 Rwandans and Burundians at the New Mwanza Hotel celebrated the assassination, leading Prime Minister John Malecela to order their arrest. This action was countermanded by the attorney general, who stated their actions were not illegal. A mourning period was also established in Zaire. President of the UN Security Council Colin Keating appealed for peace in Rwanda and Burundi and sent condolences to the families of the late presidents. Following the 6 April assassination, Juvenal Habyarimana's remains were obtained by President Mobutu of Zaire and stored in a private mausoleum in Gbadolite, Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo). Mobutu promised Habyarimana's family that his body would eventually be given a proper burial in Rwanda. On 12 May 1997, as Laurent-Désiré Kabila's ADFL rebels advanced on Gbadolite, Mobutu had the remains flown by cargo plane to Kinshasa, where they waited on the tarmac of N'djili Airport for three days. On 16 May, the day before Mobutu fled Zaire, Habyarimana's remains were cremated under the supervision of an Indian Hindu leader. The Hindu leader's presence reflected the need to cremate the body and Mobutu's insistence on a religious ceremony rather than Habyarimana's own religion. Two prominent investigations, internationally recognized, have identified the Kanombe barracks as the likely source of the missile. In 2010, the "Mutsinzi Report," carried out by Rwandan officials in collaboration with British ballistics experts from the Royal Military Academy, identified a small area including a portion of the airport, the Kanombe camp, and a small area near the presidential residence as the launch site. In January 2012, a French report was made public with similar findings. Despite these reports, some have continued to cast doubt on the conclusion. French Judge Jean-Louis Bruguière led a 2004 inquiry that accused the RPF of shooting down the plane from Masaka Hill, but it was found to be based on the testimonies of witnesses not regarded as credible. A 1994 Belgian inquiry concluded that the missile was fired from Masaka Hill, but stated it would have been virtually impossible for a rebel soldier to reach Masaka carrying missiles. The base was controlled by FAR forces, including the Presidential Guard and the para-commando battalion, and the Anti-Aircraft Battalion (LAA) were also based there. This report was widely reported to exonerate the RPF, although according to Filip Reyntjens, it did not actually do so. While initial suspicion fell on Hutu extremists who carried out the subsequent genocide, several reports since 2000 have stated that the attack was carried out by the RPF on the orders of Paul Kagame, who later became president of Rwanda. All such evidence is heavily disputed, and many academics and the United Nations have refrained from issuing a definitive finding. Mark Doyle, a BBC News correspondent who reported from Kigali during the 1994 genocide, noted in 2006 that the identities of the assassins "could turn out to be one of the great mysteries of the late 20th century." A now-declassified US Department of State intelligence report from 7 April 1994 reports an unidentified source telling the US ambassador in Rwanda that "rogue Hutu elements of the military—possibly the elite presidential guard—were responsible for shooting down the plane." This conclusion was supported by other U.S. agencies, including the Defense Intelligence Agency.

doc_name: Assassination of Juvénal Habyarimana and Cyprien Ntaryamira
text: The assassination of Rwandan President Juvénal Habyarimana and Burundian President Cyprien Ntaryamira on 6 April 1994, which triggered the Rwandan genocide, remains widely debated. Although initial suspicion focused on Hutu extremists, including figures like Colonel Théoneste Bagosora, several reports since 2000 have alleged that the RPF carried out the attack at the orders of Paul Kagame, who later became Rwanda’s president. These claims are heavily disputed, with no definitive conclusion from the United Nations or major academic institutions. A declassified U.S. Department of State report from 7 April 1994 cited an unidentified source stating that rogue Hutu military elements—possibly the elite presidential guard—were responsible, a view supported by the Defense Intelligence Agency, which reported on 9 May that the crash was an assassination by Hutu military hardliners. Philip Gourevitch, in his 1998 book, highlighted the lack of positive identification of the assassins, with Bagosora being a key suspect due to his close ties to Habyarimana and his statements about preparing an "apocalypse." The Belgian Senate’s 1997 report found insufficient information to determine specifics, while the 1998 French National Assembly report proposed two theories: Hutu extremists acting due to fears of RPF advances, or the RPF acting due to stalled Arusha Accords negotiations; it offered no definitive conclusion. The Organisation of African Unity’s 2000 report avoided assigning responsibility. In January 2000, Louise Arbour, chief prosecutor of the ICTR, terminated an investigation into the shootdown after three Tutsi informants accused Kagame and the RPF of being part of an "elite strike team," with one whistleblower, Jean-Pierre Mugabe, making a declaration in April 2000. A three-page memorandum by investigator Michael Hourigan was sent to the ICTR, and Hourigan stated he was "astounded" when Arbour reversed her position, claiming the investigation was outside her mandate; this was supported by Jim Lyons, a former FBI agent, who believed Arbour acted under orders, though Luc Reydams’ investigation concluded the decision was based on practical and legal assessments, not orders. Arbour later stated it was her personal decision, noting that the plane crash did not clearly constitute a war crime or crime against humanity under the law, and that the focus should have been on RPF actions during the genocide period. In 1998, French magistrate Jean-Louis Bruguière opened an investigation on behalf of the French crew families, concluding the attack was ordered by Kagame and issuing arrest warrants against nine of his aides in 2006; Rwanda responded by severing diplomatic ties. Bruguière’s key witness, Abdul Ruzibiza, a former RPF lieutenant, claimed involvement in the downing using SA-16 missiles and published his testimony in 2004 and a book in 2005, asserting Kagame’s responsibility; however, in November 2008 he retracted his claims, stating they were due to personal security concerns, and later claimed he did not personally participate but knew someone who did. Critics, including Linda Melvern and Colette Braeckman, questioned the reliability of Bruguière’s evidence, with Braeckman suggesting French military involvement. Kagame responded in a 2007 BBC interview by offering cooperation with an impartial, neutral inquiry, though the BBC doubted such a judge would accept the task. Paul Rusesabagina, known for his role in Hotel Rwanda, supported the theory that Kagame and the RPF were responsible, arguing it defied logic that the UN Security Council did not investigate, as it had after Rafic Hariri’s 2005 assassination. In February 2008, Spanish judge Fernando Andreu issued an 182-page indictment and international arrest warrants against 40 high-ranking RPF officials, charging them with crimes from 1990 to 2002, including the plane shootdown, based partly on universal jurisdiction. Kagame also ordered a Rwandan commission to investigate French involvement in the genocide, which issued its report in November 2007 and stated it would await Kagame’s validation. In January 2010, Rwanda released the Mutsinzi Report, which implicates Hutu Power proponents in the attack; Philip Gourevitch noted that France and Rwanda reestablished diplomatic relations shortly after Rwanda’s admission to the Commonwealth, and that the report had been shared with France prior to that, implying France’s acceptance of its findings. Ntaryamira’s death is commemorated annually in Burundi on 6 April, though it has been overshadowed by Habyarimana’s death and the subsequent genocide.
